entries.title: The work behind the credits
entries.event_semantics: 2024 is the interview publication anchor, not Pune's founding or a claim that all these jobs began that year. Corporate testimony is attributed. Published credits verify roles, not working conditions. No current headcount or generic Indian-industry claim.
entries.summary: A production director and Just Dance credits reveal Pune's contributions.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary creators, interviewers and production records credited per card.
body: Annu Koul began as a quality-control tester in 2008. By the time Ubisoft interviewed her in January 2024, she was directing production in Pune. Her account connects two jobs that a short studio description might separate: finding problems in a game and organising the people making it. She describes production through clear tasks, milestones and dependencies. A change in one part of a project can affect several others. Her responsibility was to help teams understand that chain before it disrupted their work.

Distance was part of that production problem. Koul describes coordinating with other studios across time zones, including Canadian teams on Far Cry 5. In her account, hybrid working still involved teams meeting in the studio at least twice a week, while keeping co-development partners informed. These are a manager's descriptions of her own workplace, rather than an independent assessment of every employee's experience. They make a particular skill visible: arranging when people can work together, alongside deciding what each person needs to deliver.

The published credits for Just Dance 2024 Edition offer a different view of Pune's contribution. Sanjana Akud, Gaurav Kadam and Lalit Potdar appear as dance level designers; Pooja Priolkar is credited as an associate lead level designer. The document identifies these roles and their location without reducing the studio to a single function. Reading names beside responsibilities changes the scale of the picture. A dance game presented as an immediate physical activity also contains work organised as levels, scores, technology and production.

Further down those credits, Priyanka Thombre appears in tracking, while Sarwesh Shahane is credited as QC tracking project lead. Other Pune entries cover game testing, certification, release and build work. These distinctions matter when discussing who made a game: checking compatibility is a different responsibility from designing a dance level, even when both belong to the same city. The credits do not reconstruct anyone's whole working day. They do preserve named contributions that disappear when production is described only through a publisher's logo.

entries.title: Building Aurion in Yaoundé
entries.event_semantics: No first-game, first-studio or continent-wide priority claim. Madiba's funding restrictions are his recollection of 2012, not a description of current Kickstarter rules. Mythological influences are attributed to the creator, not asserted as a complete ethnographic account.
entries.summary: How Kiro'o Games changed Aurion's tools, funding and fantasy.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary creators, interviewers and production records credited per card.
body: Olivier Madiba's account of Aurion begins with an amateur project, not a ready-made studio. In the early 2000s, he worked with Dominique Yakan and Hugues Wouafo using RPG Maker. He remembers learning staging, programming and writing while borrowing graphics from existing games. Those experiments were not the finished commercial artwork. They were a way to discover what the team could make. Madiba later moved to RPG Maker XP and began building a layer of his own technology around it, pursuing a more dynamic action game.

In his 2016 postmortem, Madiba recalls preparing a demo for a Kickstarter campaign in 2012, then discovering that he could not launch it from Cameroon. The expected route to finance was unavailable. During 2013, his group organised investment presentations locally and trained artists and programmers around the project. A prototype now had another purpose: persuading people that a professional game could actually be delivered. That account follows one team's negotiations and obstacles, rather than making a claim that game development began in Africa with Aurion.

The world inside the game changed too. In a 2017 interview, Madiba describes moving away from an early story resembling the manga and role-playing games he admired. He names research into the Ammawouli foundation and Dieudonné Iyodi's work on Bassa'a spiritual life. Contemporary political dilemmas also informed the writing. These were selected ingredients for a fictional action RPG, not a single, comprehensive African mythology. His explanation places cultural invention beside technical development: deciding what to draw from was part of deciding what game to make.

Release did not end that work. Discussing Aurion after its 2016 launch, Madiba said communication had not been handled well and that the studio needed to reach a more specific audience. He also described other Cameroonian studios, SDK Game and Noohkema, and mutual support between developers. That detail resists a solitary-pioneer story. Kiro'o's experience belongs among other efforts, with distinct teams and ambitions. The immediate question after finishing an ambitious game was how to connect it with people willing to learn its particular language of play.

entries.summary: A small team makes a father's fear playable.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary creators, interviewers and production records credited per card.
body: On his own page for Liyla and the Shadows of War, Rasheed Abueideh describes seeing images of children killed in Gaza and imagining his own family in their place. He explains the game as a way to communicate sadness, fear, empathy and anger. That is a creator stating his purpose, rather than the museum speaking for every Palestinian experience. The starting point was a parent's vulnerability. Building a game meant asking someone else to take actions inside an experience shaped by that fear.

For the 2016 release, Abueideh handled design and programming while Wedad Irshaid supplied art and Sarah Shawwa created animation. In his Gamesauce interview, he described finding his Jordanian collaborators online after producing a prototype. He worked around a full-time software job and could not pay for professional help. Communicating the required art remotely took time. The finished work's small scale therefore involved real coordination across people and places, rather than a single developer simply transferring an idea straight from imagination to a screen.

Abueideh also explained his visual decisions in that interview. Early pixel art did not fit the story he wanted to tell. Limbo offered an example of a simpler, sombre image, and he chose dark silhouettes and greys to support uncertainty and distress. The design was a deliberate response to the subject as well as to production resources. It withheld the bright reassurance of a heroic adventure. What the player could see, and what remained unclear, became part of how the game addressed its audience.

The creator's description places a family under time pressure, moving through bombing and difficult decisions in search of safety. It calls the work an appeal for help and identifies its connection to actual events. Those claims describe the work's intention; individual historical incidents still need their own evidence. The important design distinction is the role offered to the player. Liyla asks for participation in danger and uncertainty, without making that participation proof that a brief game can reproduce another person's lived experience.

entries.summary: Kingdom Rush grows across platforms through complementary skills.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary creators, interviewers and production records credited per card.
body: Ironhide describes its beginnings as three founders working in a small living room. Kingdom Rush grew from their wish to attempt something larger than their earlier projects, using a tower-defence genre they already enjoyed. The studio's history identifies the original game as a Flash production, made for web portals. That platform was a practical starting place, rather than a temporary disguise for a console game. The task was to make players feel involved in a battle while working within the team's available experience.

While the web version was being finished, Ironhide began changing the interface and other elements for iPad. Its own history recalls a push to have that version ready for Christmas 2011. The smaller iPhone display initially seemed unsuitable, but the team later found ways to adapt the game. Those decisions make a port more than a new download button. Information, touch targets and the view of a battlefield have to remain usable on the screen someone actually holds, or the familiar rules become difficult to read.

In an interview with Álvaro Azofra and Gonzalo Sande, the different jobs behind those rules become explicit. Sande argued for a group able to cover art, programming and game design, even when one person covered several responsibilities. He connected Azofra's experience with role-playing games to tower values and enemy characteristics. Azofra added that design need not belong to a single designated person. Their description turns a small team into a set of complementary skills, with balancing and presentation contributing to the same playable result.

The pair also described choosing among platforms with limited resources. Azofra said Ironhide used Flash because it was what they knew, with Xcode for iOS; Sande treated software as a tool rather than a guarantee of good design. Their advice emphasised polish, presentation and humour, and a game sized to what its makers could complete. Read in context, this is working advice from particular developers, not a universal recipe. Their success did not remove the need to decide which version, feature or opportunity deserved attention next.

entries.summary: Touch controls and cultural references shape a fictional heroine.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary creators, interviewers and production records credited per card.
body: João Brant and Lucas Mattos founded Long Hat House after meeting while studying computer science. For Dandara, they worked with artist Victor Leão and musician Thommaz Kauffman. Brant's design account starts with touchscreens: touching, giving a direction and releasing could make a complete action. Rather than place familiar controller buttons on glass, the team built around that sequence. Their heroine would attach to surfaces and jump between them. A decision about a finger's movement therefore became a rule for how a world could be explored.

Supporting gamepads created another design problem. Brant explains that the project began without a publisher or access to console self-publishing; Raw Fury later helped the team work full time and reach other platforms. The change did not make the original control problem disappear. An action designed around touching and releasing had to become comfortable with buttons and sticks. His account follows that adaptation as part of making the game, rather than treating the console version as a finished idea with a different connector attached to it.

In their Into The Spine interview, the founders recall an early soldier character whose story felt detached from their own lives. They began looking instead at familiar culture and at resistance in Brazilian history. Dandara dos Palmares became an inspiration. Yet the team also recognised the research and care that a story directly about slavery would require. They moved towards a fictional world, retaining ideas of freedom and a heroine whose name had acquired significance during development. Changing the premise was a decision about responsibility as well as identity.

The same interview describes references to things the developers encountered in daily life, school and friendships. These could make an unfamiliar game world more particular without turning it into a historical reconstruction. The founders explicitly distinguish their fictional Dandara from the person who inspired her. That boundary belongs in the interpretation of the artwork. A cultural reference may invite someone to look further, but it cannot stand in for the research, people and conflicting evidence needed to tell an actual historical life with care.

entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary creators, interviewers and production records credited per card.
body: Peter Hajba, known as Skaven, remembers the making of Second Reality as a gathering at Trug's house in Pori. A guest house provided space to work, and being together allowed Future Crew to try ideas keeping some and discarding others. In his later interview, Hajba describes a move beyond placing one impressive effect after another. The group wanted transitions and closer synchronisation with music. The technical display was also an edited sequence, whose arrangement mattered as much as the individual tricks a computer could perform.

Hajba's account gives one example of that editing. His closing music had originally accompanied a planned spaceship battle; that scene was dropped in favour of a flight through a city towards the group's logo. Music survived while its visual setting changed. He also identifies several groups, including Complex and Aggression, among the scene backgrounds later represented at Remedy. This was not one collective simply changing its sign outside a door. People brought different experiences into a workplace, and continued along different paths after it.

In a Hugi interview, Samuli Syvähuoko, known as Gore, describes his own shift from graphics towards organising and recruiting. He helped bring people into Future Crew and organised journeys and events before deciding to start a company. Remedy's first game project, Death Rally, involved collaborators from the demoscene and a working relationship with Apogee. The connection was therefore practical as well as aesthetic: knowing people's skills and bringing them together could become part of game production, alongside the ability to create an impressive image.

That change also exposed a different scale of obligation. Syvähuoko recalls Max Payne's development taking longer than expected because creating a game engine compatible with many PCs was unlike making a demo. Negotiations with 3D Realms sustained salaries and office costs as work continued towards the 2001 release. This is one participant's account, not a company history. It identifies a useful tension: confidence in building technology could start a project, while compatibility, time and paying a team determined whether it could actually be finished.

entries.summary: How Pathologic's reimagined town guides and constrains its player.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary creators, interviewers and production records credited per card.
body: In August 2016, Ice-Pick Lodge told its audience that the new Pathologic needed more time. The studio's explanation described a project changing from a modest rejuvenation into a broader reimagining, with a larger town and technical problems to solve in Unity. The announcement moved the expected release to autumn 2017; it was a forecast, not the eventual date. Reading that distinction matters. A studio's public plan records what it thought possible at a particular moment, alongside the promises its team was trying to keep.

The same announcement offered a smaller playable piece made for Gamescom. Ice-Pick said it was not an alpha of the whole game: it used a separate story, omitted mechanics and contained material that would not appear in the final release. More polishing was needed before backers could play without developers explaining it beside them. A demonstration had become its own design task. It needed to convey mood and setting while standing on its own, rather than relying on someone from the team to fill its gaps.

After Pathologic 2's release, the developers described another way of guiding players. Alexandra Golubeva recalled wanting fewer direct instructions and quest markers. Twyrine, a drink that could reveal directions, and children's stashes with notes developed into ways of discovering events. A detail first added for flavour could grow into a quest. In this account, narrative design was not only the writing of dialogue. It also arranged how a player found something, and how much of the town could remain uncertain while they searched.

Quest designer Denys Surdeykin's account also identifies a limit to that ambition. Combat could express choices about violence and mercy, but restricted stealth reduced the situations the team could construct. Other developers described keeping walking and awkward combat because they wanted those pressures to mean something. These statements are not proof that every difficulty was intentional or successful. They show colleagues distinguishing an expressive rule from an implementation that constrained their work, and explaining why remaking a game involved more than improving how its streets looked.

entries.summary: Watching and playing share a room.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary creators, interviewers and production records credited per card.
body: Kook Kibong, known as TheBOy, recalls first finding his friends playing StarCraft in an internet café in Australia in 1998. He returned to watch before beginning himself. In Blizzard's later interview, this encounter sits beside memories of competing at Daytona USA machines and studying how to shave fractions from a lap time. The route into a strategy game did not begin with an isolated purchase. Other people, an available machine and the opportunity to watch made a new kind of play visible to him.

Kibong describes building a reputation on Battle.net, acquiring a manager and sponsor, and preparing strategies through repeated games and written notes. His memory of Korea's 1999 competitive scene includes television appearances and a first live tournament. These are recollections of one professional, rather than evidence that everyone entering a PC room wanted the same career. They connect several activities that a software description leaves apart: practising, learning from opponents, being watched and becoming recognisable to an audience gathered around the game and its players.

A contemporary Blizzard notice records another use of a PC bang nearly two decades later. For StarCraft: Remastered's 2017 Korean preview, the company invited adults to Gameinus's Sinnonhyeon location in Seoul. The planned evening combined a broadcast of the launch event with overnight play, individual and team tournaments, and invited broadcaster matches. This was a specifically organised gathering, not a description of every café's normal routine. Its programme placed watching and playing in the same venue, allowing one activity to lead into the next.

The announcement also specified its boundaries: registration, a limited attendance selected by lottery, identification checks and an event running beyond the hours when minors could enter. Free overnight access was part of that particular promotion. Those details show a room managed by rules and schedules as well as by networked computers. They cannot establish where PC bangs first appeared or explain their whole history. They do preserve an example of a shared gaming space being used to stage a collective occasion around a game.
